Ó tún tẹ̀síwájú pé ní ẹnu wákàtí bíi mélòó kan sẹ́yìn, òun rí i wípé gbogbo ara rẹ̀ ó sùú, tí ó sì tún dákú, kò sì tún fìdí rẹ̀ múlẹ̀ pé gbogbo eté rẹ̀ náà kò tún dunjú mọ́, ó sì ń yọ ọkùnrin, sọ́mọ náà kò sì tún lè gbé oúnjẹ kankan mì. Ó wá ń béèrè lọ́wọ́ dókítà pé, ǹjẹ́ àìsàn bẹ́ẹ̀ ṣe ṣeé tọ́jú, ó farajọ àrùn èyí, ó tún tẹ̀síwájú pé ǹjẹ́ òun lè gba bẹ́rẹ́, tàbí lo òògùn ibò sí àrùn èyí? Ó tún tẹ̀síwájú sí i pé, àgbò, ọṣẹ ìbílẹ̀, òun ni àwọn máa ń tọ́jú àrùn èyí fún kíkì ọmọ tí ó bá mú ní àyíká tí òun ti wá.
model_answer:
This most likely sounds like measles, especially with fever, cough, red eyes/rash, and poor feeding, but the child must be examined urgently to rule out pneumonia, malaria, sepsis, or severe allergic rash.  
Do not rely on traditional herbs or black soap, as they can irritate the skin, delay proper care, or cause poisoning.  
Take the child to a hospital/clinic now for assessment, fever control, fluids/feeding support, vitamin A, and treatment of complications; antibiotics or injections are only needed if there is a bacterial complication such as pneumonia or ear infection.  
Keep the child away from other children because measles spreads easily, and ensure vaccination for contacts who are not immunized.

question: ọmọ kan le wa to ṣẹ̀ṣẹ̀ bímọ tuntun ní ọ̀sẹ̀ méjì sẹ́yìn ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ díẹ̀díẹ̀ ní ojú ara rẹ̀ ṣùgbọ́n bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ ń ṣàkíyèsí pé nǹkan bí ìpin jáde nígbà mí àwọ̀ rẹ̀ yàtọ̀ ó sì ní oòrùn tí kò dára Ó sì ńá máa ń ní ìrora kékeré ní ìsàlẹ̀ ikùn rẹ̀ ní gbogbo ìgbà tó bá ń rí àmì wọ̀nyí ọkàn rẹ̀ máa ń dàrú ó ń ronú bóyá èyí jẹ́ nǹkan nínú àwọn ìṣòro tó wọ́pọ̀ lẹ́yìn ìbímọ tàbí ìṣòro ìmí ọjọ́ kan nígbà tó lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn tó ń bá àwọn ìyá mìíràn sọ̀rọ̀ Ó gbọ́ pé kò yẹ kí wọ́n fojú tẹmẹ́lú àyípadà kankan tí wọ́n bá rí ní ara wọn èyí mú kí ó pinnu láti rí dókítà láti bá wọn sọ̀rọ̀ ìbéèrè mi ní pé kí ni ó lè fa aró nǹkan yìí lẹ́yìn ìbímọ ìrora ní ìsàlẹ̀ i jẹ́? Kini awọn aami ewu ti iyamọ tuntun yi yẹ ki o ma ṣọra fun ibimọ kini awọn igbese imototo ti iya ọmọ naa ni lati telu lati dènà àìsàn lẹ́yìn ìbímọ?
reference: Ìyá ọmọ kan ní ìwà tó ṣe bí ọmọ tútùn, ní ọ̀sẹ̀ méjì sẹ́yìn. Ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ díẹ̀-díẹ̀ ní ojú ara rẹ̀. Ṣùgbọ́n bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ, ó ń sàkíyèsí pé ǹkan bí ikun àti ẹ̀jẹ̀ wá ń jáde. Nígbà mìíràn ìyá ọmọ rẹ̀ yí yàtọ̀. Ó sì ní ọrùn tí kò dára. Ó sì mọ pé ìyá ọmọ náà ma ń ní ìrora kékeré nì ìṣàlẹ̀ ikùn rẹ̀, ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá rí àmì wọ̀nyí, ọkàn rẹ̀ má ń dáru. Ó rò nù bóyá ẹ̀yì jẹ́ ǹkan nínú àwọn ìṣòro tó wọ́pọ̀ lẹ́yìn ìbímọ tàbí ìṣòro mìíràn. Ní ọjọ́ kan nígbà tó lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, tó n bá àwọn ìyá mìíràn sọ̀rọ̀, ó gbọ́ pé kò yẹ kí wọn fojú tẹ́nbẹ́lú àyípadà kankan tí wọn bá rí ní ara wọn. Èyí mú kí ó wá rí dókítà láti bá wọn sọ̀rọ̀. Ìbéèrè mí ní pè, kíní ó léè fa irú ǹkan yìí lẹ́yìn ìbímọ? Ṣé ìrora nì ìṣàlẹ̀ ikùn lè jẹ́ àmì àrùn kan? Kíní àwọn àmì wo tí ìyá ọmọ tútù yìí yẹ kí ó ma ṣọ́ra fún, lẹ́yìn ìbímọ? Kíní àwọn ìbèsèyí ìyá mọ́ tó ní láti tẹ́mọ́ láti dẹ́mọ́ àìsàn yìí?
model_answer:
This may be postpartum infection (puerperal sepsis/endometritis), especially because the discharge has a bad smell and there is lower abdominal pain; retained pieces of placenta or blood clots, infected tears/episiotomy, or poor hygiene can also cause it.  
She should go to a hospital urgently for examination, temperature check, pelvic assessment, and treatment, usually antibiotics and sometimes evacuation if retained products are present.  
Danger signs after delivery include fever or chills, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding or large clots, worsening lower abdominal pain, dizziness/fainting, severe headache/blurred vision, swollen painful leg, chest pain/shortness of breath, painful urination, or breast redness with fever.  
To prevent infection, she should wash hands before touching the genital area or baby, change maternity pads often, wash the perineum with clean water and wipe front-to-back, keep wounds clean and dry, avoid douching or inserting herbs/cloth/fingers into the vagina, and avoid sex until bleeding stops and she is medically fit.  
She should also attend postnatal clinic, take prescribed medicines fully, eat well, drink clean water, and seek care early if symptoms worsen.

question: Ọmọ mi ọmọ mi obìnrin wà nínú oyún ó ti le ní ogó ọdún ó lé merin ló wà nínú eyín àtigbà tí ó ti di ọdun ó di ọdọ mi ní ìjẹta yẹn báyìí nígbà tó máa di omí mo ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní mu ó sì ti kọ́. Mo gbogbo eru re o ti ko wa sọ mi omo yin mo ṣayin pe o n mu fi silẹ mo ba sadi gbogbo eru re pe o ja ma lo si ile-iwosan a ba samu de ile iwosan ba mi yewo wọn sọ pe ile omo ti ṣi o ti n ṣe bodie naa loku ti o fi ṣetan ti o ma di ana omo lo so di omo. bo nijẹta di ana ọmọ náà sì wà ní ibi tó ti ń rọbí láti ìjẹta ó ń rọbí ọmọ òsì bota omo alakobi si mi alakobi re si lube lo wa to ti n robi latanu omo obota egun si n ba mi aya mi n ja mi ifẹ padanu omo mi si fe padanu omo to n bo naa Lako kini nkan to fa omo naa to fi wa n ro bi to pepepe ma n se awon alakobi ni o ba fe bimo ni abi se omo naa se ose ko jẹ ki bi o ti tobi ju ti o wa le gba ibi oju ara omo mi yii ni abi se ose ko jẹ pe wọn maa se abe fun omo naa tori

Ọmọ mi obìnrin wà nínú oyún, ó ti lè jẹ́ ọmọ ọdún mẹ́rìnlélógún. Òun ni ó wà nínú oyún. Lónìí ni ìṣẹ̀lẹ̀ yìí ṣẹlẹ̀.
Nígbà tí ó di alẹ́, mo ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ náà bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ní ìrora. Ó sì ti kó ẹrù rẹ̀, ó ti wá sí ilé mi. Bí ìrora ṣe ń lọ, mo rí i pé ó ń pọ̀ sí i. Mo kó gbogbo ẹrù rẹ̀ jọ, kò sì jẹ́ kí a lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀.
A gbé e dé ilé ìwòsàn, wọ́n sì ṣàyẹ̀wò rẹ̀. Wọ́n sọ pé ilé-ọmọ ti bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ṣí díẹ̀, àti pé kù díẹ̀ ni yóò tó ìgbà ìbímọ.
Ní òní ṣáájú, ilé-ọmọ ṣi ń ṣí sí i títí dé ìgbà tí ọmọ yóò fi bọ̀. Nígbà tí ó di ana, ọmọ náà wà nínú ìrora tí ó ń túbọ̀ ń pọ̀ sí i láti ìgbà tí a dé ibẹ̀.
Ó ń ní ìrora, ọmọ yóò sì bọ̀, ọmọ àkọ́bí ni. Ẹ̀rù sì ń bà mí, ọkàn sì ń bà mí.
Mo fẹ́ gba ọmọ mi là, mi ò sì fẹ́ pàdánù ọmọ tí ń bọ̀. Ẹ jọ̀wọ́, kí ni ó lè fà ìrora yìí tí ó ń ń lọ báyìí? Ṣé bó ṣe máa ń rí fún àwọn alábọ̀bí ni yẹn nígbà tí wọ́n fẹ́ bí? Ṣé ó ṣeé ṣe kó jẹ́ pé ọmọ náà ti tóbi jù, tí kò lè jáde lọ́nà ìbímọ? Tàbí ṣé ó ṣeé ṣe kó jẹ́ pé wọ́n máa ṣe iṣẹ́ abẹ fún un?
model_answer:
This sounds like prolonged or obstructed labour, which is an emergency, especially if she has been in labour for many hours/days or her waters have broken.  
Common causes include a baby that is too big for the mother’s pelvis, poor baby position, weak contractions, or the cervix not opening well; it is more common in first pregnancies but it is not normal to “keep trying” for days.  
She needs urgent assessment in a hospital with capability for Caesarean section, blood transfusion, antibiotics, and fetal monitoring, because delay can lead to loss of the baby, heavy bleeding, infection, ruptured womb, or death of the mother.  
If the cervix is not progressing, the baby is distressed, or the baby cannot pass through the birth canal, Caesarean section is the correct and lifesaving treatment.  
Please do not manage this at home or with a traditional birth attendant—take her immediately to a proper hospital or request referral now.

question: Àgbàlagbà kan ló wá sí ilé ìwòsàn alábọ́dé Baba wa yìí sọ wípé orí fò àwọn gan tí ọran wọn sì lè tí àwọn sì rí kòkòrò kan lójijì tí ó ṣú sí àwọn ní ara àwọn wà láti béèrè nǹkan tí ó lè fa àti pé irú ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún àwọn? Dókítà wà ní wípé kí ló lè fa irú àìsàn orí fífọ́ orùn líle àti tí bàbá yìí kò lè yí ọrùn tí kòkòrò sì bò wọ́n ní gbogbo ara kí ló lè fa àrùn èyí ni eléyìí ni àbí nǹkan mìíràn? péye àti wípé ògùn wo lalẹ̀ ni kí baba yìí ló kí? ayéwò wọn tó dé
reference:
Bàbá àgbàlagbà kan ni wọ́n wá sí ilé ìwòsàn alábòde wa. Bàbá yìí sọ pé orí ń fò ó gan-an, ọrùn rẹ̀ sì le, ó sì ní kokoro kan ní ojijì tí ó sú sí i ní ara. Ó wá láti béèrè ohun tí ó lè fà á àti irú ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún un.
A béèrè lọ́wọ́ bàbá yìí pé ṣé orí náà bẹ̀rẹ̀ lójijì ni tàbí pé ó ti ń fò ó díẹ̀díẹ̀. Bàbá náà sì sọ pé lójijì ni ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ ní òru, ó sì ti lágbára gan-an báyìí. A tún béèrè lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ pé ṣé ó lè wo ìmọ́lẹ̀ dáadáa, bàbá náà sì sọ pé rárá, kò lè wo ìmọ́lẹ̀ nítorí pé ó máa ń wọ agbárí rẹ̀, tí orí náà sì tún máa ń fò ó sí i.
A tún béèrè lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ pé kokoro tí ó ń mú un yìí, ṣé ó ń le tàbí ó pọ̀, tàbí pé ó fẹ́rẹ̀fẹ́ ni. Bàbá náà sọ pé gbogbo ara òun ni, kò sì lè mọ ibi pàtó, ṣùgbọ́n ó ń yún un.
Lẹ́yìn náà, a béèrè lọ́wọ́ bàbá náà pé ṣé ó ní ìbáṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú aláìsàn kankan láìpẹ́ yìí, bàbá náà sì sọ pé wọn kò lọ sí ibi kankan ju pé wọ́n tà ọjà ní iwájú ilé wọn. Wọ́n kò sì ní ìfarakànra pẹ̀lú aláìsàn kankan.
Ìbéèrè wa fún dókítà ni pé kí ni ó lè fà irú àìsàn orífífó àti ọrùn líle tí bàbá yìí kò lè yí ọrùn rẹ̀, tí kokoro sì bò ó ní gbogbo ara? Kí ló lè fà á? Ṣé àrùn ẹyí ni èyí tàbí nǹkan míì?
Ìbéèrè wa kejì ni pé irú àyẹ̀wò wo ni a lè ní kí bàbá yìí ṣe láti mọ ohun tí ń ṣe é ní pàtó fún ìtọ́jú tó péye, àti pé oogun wo ni a lè ní kí bàbá yìí lò kí èsì àyẹ̀wò rẹ̀ tó dé?
model_answer: This is a medical emergency most consistent with acute meningitis, possibly meningococcal meningitis/septicaemia, because of sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and a widespread rash. Do not wait for test results: admit or urgently refer, check vital signs and blood glucose, give oxygen/IV fluids if needed, and take blood culture and malaria test only if they do not delay treatment. Start ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM every 12 hours immediately; in an elderly patient add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours if available to cover Listeria. Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, plus paracetamol for fever/pain, and avoid lumbar puncture if there is coma, seizures, focal weakness, papilloedema, or shock until stabilized. Isolate the patient and give close household contacts prophylaxis according to local protocol, such as ciprofloxacin single dose, if meningococcal disease is suspected.

question: Ìyàwó kan lori wipe oko re wupọ gan ni gbogbo aarọ nigba ji lori ibusun ikona ma n bẹrẹ lẹsẹkẹsẹ o si maa n gba akoko lati dawo duro bi ọjọ ṣe n lo o tu ri pe oko re n tiraka lati mi dada nigbamii bi o ba rin jinna diẹ tabi gun atẹgun o maa n duro. láti gba ìmí rẹ̀ padà ó tún máa rẹ́ kíákíá ní alẹ́ ọjọ́ kan lẹ́yìn tí ọkọ rẹ̀ lo ìgbà pípẹ́ láti wúkọ́ àti láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà inú ìyàwó náà bàjẹ́ ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń ronú bóyá àrùn kan wà lẹ́ tí ó ń fa gbogbo àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí. reference:
Ìyàwó kan rí i pé ọkọ rẹ̀ ń wúkọ́ gan-an nígbà tí wọ́n bá jí ní orí ibùsùn. Ikọ́ náà máa ń bẹ̀rẹ̀ lójijì, ó sì máa ń gba àkókò kí ó tó dáwọ́ dúró. Ní ọjọ́ kan, lẹ́yìn tí ọkọ rẹ̀ gba àkókò pípẹ́ láti wúkọ́ àti láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà, inú ìyàwó náà bàjẹ́. Ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í rò pé bóyá àrùn kan wà tí ń fa gbogbo àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí. Ní ọjọ́ kejì, ó bá ọkọ rẹ̀ sọ̀rọ̀ pé kí wọ́n lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, kí wọ́n lè rí dókítà, kí wọ́n lè mọ ohun tí ń ṣẹlẹ̀ gan-an.
Ìbéèrè ni pé kí ni ó lè fà kí ikọ́ ní agbára tó bẹ́ẹ̀, kí ara ẹni máa rẹ̀ ní gbogbo ìgbà, kí ènìyàn tún ní ìṣòro mímí dáadáa nígbà gbogbo tí ikọ́ bá ń wáyé? Ṣé ìṣòro yìí lè ní ṣe pẹ̀lú àrùn ẹdọforo tàbí àrùn ọkàn nìkan? Kí ni àwọn ohun tí ó lè mú ikú wá, kí ó sì jẹ́ kí ènìyàn máa tiraka láti mí, tí ó sì lewu débi pé ènìyàn gbọ́dọ̀ tètè lọ ṣàyẹ̀wò?
Kí ni àwọn àmi ewu mímí tí ìdílé gbọ́dọ̀ máa ṣọ́ra fún nípa ikọ́ àti ìṣòro mímí?
model_answer:
A strong cough every morning with breathlessness on walking or climbing stairs is commonly seen in chronic bronchitis/COPD, especially in smokers or people exposed to cooking smoke, dust, or fumes.  
Other important causes include asthma, tuberculosis, pneumonia, heart failure, post-nasal drip, or acid reflux, so it is not only “lung disease”; heart disease can also cause cough and shortness of breath.  
He should be examined at a hospital for chest assessment, oxygen level, sputum testing for TB, chest X-ray, and possibly lung function tests.  
Danger signs needing urgent care include breathlessness at rest, blue lips, chest pain, coughing blood, high fever, night sweats, weight loss, confusion/fainting, swollen legs, or inability to speak full sentences.  
If he smokes, stopping smoking and avoiding smoke/dust exposure is very important while awaiting medical review.

question: Ọ̀kan lára àwọn olóyún wa la rí ní àfẹ̀mọjúmọ̀ yìí pẹ̀lú ọkọ̀ wọn, wọ́n sọ wípé àwọn ní ìrora tí ó lágbára ni inú àwọn tí ẹ̀yin sì ń rú àwọn tí kò sì tí tó ọjọ́ ìbí àwọn abìnrin wabìnrin pé oyún oṣù mélòó ni wọ́n ní tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún oṣù mẹ́fà àti ọjọ́ díẹ̀ a tún wá bẹ̀ wípé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ àbí ohun ò ń fi wọ́n sì sọ pé àwọn ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ nígbà náà ni abo arabìnrin. wí pé njẹ wọn rí omi àbí ẹ̀jẹ̀ san sọ wípé àmúrí omi amọ sì rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ àtúnwá bèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ọmọkeló ní oyún ti wọn ni wọn oyún eleke lo ni oyún tí ó wà nínú tó ń sọ wípé oyún alákọ́èrè wa fún dókítà wa ní wípé mi lè jẹ́ lè tọ́ka sí ààmí ìrọ̀bí àbí àmì wípé oyún bájìn mìíràn ǹjẹ́ a lè sọ? arábìnrin yẹn lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò fọ́tò inú, ilé ìta ń pè ní san láti mú nǹkan tí ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀.
reference: Ọ̀kan lára àwọn olóyún wa la rí ní àfẹ̀mojúmọ yìí pẹ̀lú ọkọ wọn, wọ́n sọ wípé àwọn ní ìrora tí ó lágbára ní inú àwọn tí ẹ̀yìn sì ń ro àwọn, tí kò sì tíì tó ọjọ́ ìbí àwọn. A béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí pé oyún oṣù mélòó ni wọ́n ní, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún oṣù mẹ́fà àti ọjọ́ díẹ̀. A tún wá béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí pé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ àbí ó mú wọn, ó ń fi wọ́n sílẹ̀, wọ́n sì ní àwọn ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́. Nígbà náà ni a béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n rí omi àbí rí ẹ̀jẹ̀, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé àwọn rí omi àti ẹ̀jẹ̀. A tún wá béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ọmọ ẹlẹ́kẹlo, oyún ẹlẹ́kẹlo ni oyún tí ó wà nínú wọn, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún àlá kọ kọ́. Ìbéèrè wa fún dókítà wa ni pé ǹjẹ́ àmì yìí lè tọ́ka sí àmì ìrọbí àbí àmì wípé oyún bàjẹ́ àbí àmì míràn? Ǹjẹ́ a lè sọ wípé kí arábìnrin yìí lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò fọ́tò inú rẹ̀ tí a ń pè ní <codeswitch> <English> scan láti mọ nǹkan tí ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀?
model_answer:
Yes, this is an obstetric emergency: at about 6 months pregnancy, severe abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding or watery discharge may indicate preterm labour, premature rupture of membranes, placental abruption, or late miscarriage.  
She should be sent immediately to a hospital with maternity/emergency obstetric care; do not manage her at home or delay for routine ultrasound.  
Assessment should include vital signs, abdominal and speculum examination, fetal heartbeat, ultrasound, and tests for bleeding, infection, and blood group/Rhesus status.  
If the baby is viable, treatment may include steroids for the baby’s lungs, magnesium sulfate, antibiotics if membranes have ruptured, and careful decision on whether to stop labour or deliver depending on mother and baby’s condition.  
Heavy bleeding, severe constant pain, fever, fainting, or reduced fetal movement are danger signs requiring urgent action.

question: Dókítà ìyẹ ọmọkùnrin tó ń gbé ní ilé wa ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ṣe àkíyèsí pé ọmọ rẹ̀ kò mọ ọmú dáadáa ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá gbìyànjú láti fún ní ọmọ náà máa mú díẹ̀ lẹ́yìn náà ó máa dáwọ́ dúró bí ẹni pé ó rẹ́ ọmọ náà tóbi pé ọmọ náà ò ní agbára láti mu ọmú ó sì máa ń làágùn púpọ̀ lórí àti ní ojú rẹ̀ kì í ṣe èyí. nìkan èmi rẹ̀ ó yí padà o máa ń dàbí pé ó ń mi lọ sókè o ń mí lọ sísàlẹ̀ bí ẹni tó ń tiraka láti mí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ ìyá ọmọ náà túbọ̀ ń bẹ̀rù ó ń wò bóyá torí pé ọmọ náà ò jẹ́ ohun tó ni àbí bóyá ó ní ìṣòro kan nípa èyí àti bó ṣe ń láàgùn nítorí náà ó pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láti rí dókítà fún. wò ọmọ náà ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fàá kí ọmọ máa ń ní ìṣòro láti mu ọmú dáadáa náà ṣe mí jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera kankan tí òbí ọmọ náà ní kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún ló lè fa? Bí ọmọdé máa làágùn nígbà tó bá ń mu omú.
reference:
Dokita, iya ọmọ kan tó ń gbé ní ilé wa, ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ rẹ kò mu ọmú dáadáa. Ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá gbìyànjú láti fún un ní ọmú, ọmọ náà máa mu díẹ̀, lẹ́yìn náà ó máa dáwọ́ dúró bí ẹni pé ó rẹ̀ẹ́. Ìyá ọmọ náà tún rí pé ọmọ náà kò ní agbára láti mu ọmú, ó sì máa ń làágùn púpọ̀ lórí àti ní ojú rẹ̀. Kì í ṣe èyí nìkan, èémí rẹ̀ ó yí padà, ó máa ń dàbí pé ó ń mí lọ sókè, ó ń mí lọ sísàlẹ̀, bí ẹni tó ń tiraka láti mí. Bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ, ìyá ọmọ náà ń túbọ̀ ń bẹ̀rù, ó ń wo bóyá torí pé ọmọ náà kò jẹun tó ni, àbí bóyá ó ní ìṣòro kan nípa èémí àti bóyá ṣe ń làágùn. Nítorí náà, ó pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn. Láti rí dókítà fún àyẹ̀wò ọmọ náà. Ìbéèrè mi ni wípé kí ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ máa ní ìṣòro láti mu ọmú dáadáa? Ṣé bí ọmọ náà ṣe ń mí jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera kankan? Kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tí òbí ọmọ náà ní kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún? Kí ló lè fa kí ọmọ kékeré máa làágùn nígbà tí ó bá ń mu ọmú?
English Translation
model_answer:
Sweating and tiring during breastfeeding, especially with fast or laboured breathing, is a warning sign and can be due to congenital heart disease causing heart failure in the baby.  
Other possible causes include pneumonia or other chest infection, severe anaemia, prematurity/low birth weight, poor latch, or metabolic problems, but the combination of sweating, breathlessness and poor feeding needs urgent medical assessment.  
Parents should watch for bluish lips or tongue, breathing faster than normal, chest indrawing, poor weight gain, swelling, fever, extreme sleepiness, or passing little urine.  
The baby should be taken to a hospital promptly for examination, oxygen level check, weight assessment, chest/heart evaluation, and possibly echocardiography.  
Until reviewed, feed in small frequent amounts and keep the baby upright, but do not delay seeking care.

question: ọmọ kan yóò ṣàkíyèsí fún ọjọ́ díẹ̀ báyìí ọmọ yẹn bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní wúkọ́ láì dáwọ́ dúró ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀ kúrò pé òtútù lóko sọmọ náà láyà pé ó máa lọ ṣùgbọ́n ikọ́ náà kò dínkù ní gbogbo alẹ́ ọmọ náà máa jí nílòji nítorí ikọ́ nígbà mi ó máa ń wù wá bẹ́ẹ̀ ni pé ó ṣò. Gbogbo fún láti lè mí dáadáa máa gbé sókè ó sì máa gbọ́ bí àyà rẹ̀ ṣe ń ṣiṣẹ́ nígbà tó bá mú èyí ń mu kí ọmọ náà máa lè sùn dáadáa ní alẹ́ ní ọjọ́ kan lẹ́yìn alẹ́ tí ọmọ náà tó wúkọ́ gan tó sì tiraka láti lè mí dáadáa ìyá rẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ sí. Ilé ìwòsàn ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa iko náà àti ìṣòro tó fi ń tó fa láti mí dáadáa àti bí ó ṣe lè rán ọmọ náà lọ́wọ́ béèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ máa wuko gan kò sì ní ìṣòro láti lè mí dáadáa pàápàá ní alẹ́ kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tó yẹ kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra? Fún nígbà tí ọmọ náà bá ń wúkọ́ àwọn nǹkan wo ló yẹ kí wọ́n yàgò fún láti dènà ikọ yìí?
reference:
Ìyá ọmọ kan ló ṣàkíyèsí wípé fún ọjọ́ díẹ̀ báyìí, pé ọmọ òun bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í wúkọ láì dáwọ́ dúró. Ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀, ó rò pé òtútù ló kọ ọmọ náà láyà, pé ó máa lọ. Ṣùgbọ́n ikọ́ náà kò dínkù. Ní gbogbo alẹ́, ọmọ náà máa jí lójijì nítorí ikọ́. Nígbà míì, ó máa ń wíwá bí ẹni pé ó ṣòro fún un láti mí dáadáa. Ìyá rẹ̀ máa gbé e sókè, ó sì máa gbọ́ bí àyà rẹ̀ ṣe ń ṣiṣẹ́ nígbà tí ó bá ń mí. Èyí mú kí ọmọ náà má lè sùn dáadáa ní alẹ́.
Ní ọjọ́ kan, lẹ́yìn alẹ́ tí ọmọ náà ti wúkọ gan-an tí ó sì tiraka láti mí dáadáa, ìyá rẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn. Ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa ikọ́ náà àti ìṣòro tó fa láti má lè mí dáadáa, àti bí ó ṣe lè ràn án lọ́wọ́.
Ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ló lè fa kí ọmọ máa wúkọ gan, kí ó sì ní ìṣòro láti mí dáadáa pàápàá ní alẹ́? Kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tí ó yẹ kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún nígbà tí ọmọ náà bá ń wúkọ? Àwọn nǹkan wo ló yẹ kí wọ́n yàgò fún láti dènà ikọ́ yìí?
model_answer:
A child with persistent cough worse at night plus wheezing or “chest working hard” may have asthma/reactive airway disease triggered by a viral cold, dust or smoke, but pneumonia, bronchiolitis, whooping cough, TB, or an inhaled foreign body must also be considered.  
Because the child is struggling to breathe, they should be examined urgently at a hospital for respiratory rate, oxygen level, chest signs, and treatment such as inhaled salbutamol/nebulization, oxygen, or antibiotics only if indicated.  
Danger signs are fast breathing, chest indrawing, noisy breathing/stridor, blue lips, inability to drink or breastfeed, extreme weakness/drowsiness, convulsions, persistent high fever, vomiting everything, or cough lasting more than 2 weeks with weight loss/night sweats.  
To reduce attacks, avoid cigarette smoke, cooking smoke/charcoal or kerosene fumes, dust, strong perfumes/insecticides, cold air, mold, and known triggers such as pets or certain foods if clearly linked.  
Do not give adult medicines, leftover antibiotics, or sedating cough mixtures; keep the child upright, offer fluids, and follow the clinician’s plan including inhaler technique if asthma is diagnosed.

question: Ọmọ mi ẹni ọdún mẹ́sàn ni mo gbé wá sí ilé ìwòsàn ní ọ̀sán yìí mo ná ọmọ náà níṣẹ́ láti ra nǹkan fún mi ní ìgboro ṣùgbọ́n a já bu ọmọ náà jẹ nígbà tí wọ́n mú ọmọ náà délé tí wọ́n sì ṣàlàyé fún mi tó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ọmọ náà mo wo ojú egbò tí ajá ti bu ọmọ náà jẹ mo rí pé ojú egbò náà pọ́n ó sì ti wú a ṣe ìwádìí ládùgbò láti mor tó ọmọ náà jẹ́ olówó ajá náà sì sọ wípé àwọn kò gba abere fún ajá náà rí pé lẹ́yìn kí ó jáde kó ṣeré kó sì padà wọlé, wọ́n ní àwọn ogbà ìtọ́jú kankan fún ajá náà rì ni ẹ̀rù ṣe bà mí láti gbé ọmọ náà wá sí ilé ìwòsàn kó má jẹ́ wípé ajá tó bu ọmọ náà jẹ́ ó jẹ́ ajá digbolugi Kí ló ṣeéṣe kó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ọmọ tí a já bùjẹ? Kí ló ṣeéṣe kí ó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ojú egbò tí ó ń pọ́n tí ó sì ń wú? N ó ṣe kí ẹran ipá tí ẹ ti wọnú egbò yìí ó ṣe kí ọmọ náà kó kí nǹkan kó ṣe ọmọ. Ọmọ náà látàrí ọmọ tí a já wo ni mo lè ṣe láti má jẹ́ kí ẹran ipa wọnú egbò yìí awọn abẹ́rẹ́ wo àwọn oògùn a lè fi tọ́jú ọmọdé yìí láti jẹ́ kó ní ìtọ́jú tó péye. Àwọn ohun wo ni a tún lè ṣe tàbí ayewo lale ṣe láti tọju oju egbo ti a ja ti ọmọde.
reference:
Ọmọ mi ẹni ọdun mẹsan ni mo gbe wa si ile-iwosan ni ọsan yi. Mo ran ọmọ naa ni iṣẹ lati ra nkan fun mi ni igboro, ṣugbọn aja bu ọmọ naa jẹ. Nigba ti wọn mu ọmọ naa dele, ti wọn si ṣalaye fun mi ohun to ṣẹlẹ si ọmọ naa, mo wo oju egbo ti aja ti bu ọmọ naa jẹ, mo ri pe oju egbo naa pọn, o si ti wú. A ṣe iwadi ni adugbo lati mọ irú aja to bu ọmọ naa jẹ, olowo aja naa si sọ wipe awọn kò gba abẹrẹ fun aja naa rí, wipe lẹyin ki o jade, ko ṣere, ko si pada wọle. Wọn ni awọn o gba itọju kankan fun aja naa rí. Idi eyi ni ẹru ṣe bami lati gbe ọmọ naa wa si ile-iwosan, ko ma jẹ wipe aja to bu ọmọ naa jẹ, o jẹ aja digbolugi. Ki lo ṣeṣe ko ṣẹlẹ si ọmọ ti aja bu jẹ yi? Ki lo ṣeṣe ko ṣẹlẹ si oju egbo ti o n pọn, ti o si n wú? N jẹ o ṣeṣe ki ẹran ipa ti ẹ ti wọnu egbo yi? N jẹ o ṣeṣe ki ọmọ naa... ki nkan ko ṣe ọmọ naa latari ọmọ ti aja bu jẹ? Ẹ jọọ...
Awọn wo ni mo le ṣe lati ma jẹ ki ẹran ipa wọnu egbo yi? Awọn abẹrẹ wo, awọn ogun wo ni a le fi tọju ọmọde yi lati jẹ ko ni itọju to peye? Awọn wo ni a tun le ṣe tabi ayẹwo wo la le ṣe lati tọju oju egbo ti aja ti bu ọmọde yi jẹ?
model_answer:
A bite from an unvaccinated dog is high risk for rabies and wound infection; rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so treatment must start immediately, without waiting to see if the dog becomes sick.  
The red, swollen wound suggests inflammation or cellulitis from bacteria in the dog’s mouth, and the child also needs tetanus protection.  
Wash the wound thoroughly with running water and soap for at least 15 minutes, apply povidone-iodine/chlorhexidine, remove dead tissue/foreign material, and avoid tight primary stitching unless a clinician decides it is necessary.  
Give rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, and 14, plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound if this is a deep/transdermal bite or saliva entered broken skin.  
The child should also receive tetanus vaccine/immune globulin as indicated, antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5–7 days, pain relief, and assessment for pus, abscess, tendon/nerve injury, fracture or foreign body, with X-ray/culture if needed.

question: Alágbà tó ṣàkíyèsí wípé ọmọ náà ń wúkọ́ gidigidi débi pé ó ń ta gì pé ọmọ náà gbìyànjú tiraka láti mí dáradára ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ kí ó máa wúkó àtarìbi wí pé kò lè mí dáadáa tó ń tiraka láti mi irú ni a lè ṣe fún ọmọ náà ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún Bákan náà irú ìmọ̀ràn wo ni a lè gba ìyá ọ lágbà ìtọ́jú ọmọdé náà?
reference: Alágbàtọ́ ọmọ kan ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ náà wúkọ́ gidigidi, dé bi pé òun tàgìrì àti wí pé ọmọ náà gbìyànjú tiraka láti mí dáradára ni. Kí ó le fa kí ọmọ kí ó máa n wúkọ́ àwú tagìrì, débi wípé kò le mí dáadáa, tó tiraka láti mí? Irú àyẹ̀wò wo la lè ṣe fún ọmọ náà? Irú ìtọ́jú wo la lè fún? Bákan náà irú àmọ̀rà wo la lè gba Alágbàtọ́ ọmọ náà?
model_answer:
Severe cough with struggling to breathe in a child can be caused by pneumonia, asthma/bronchiolitis, croup, whooping cough, or choking/foreign body aspiration, and it is a medical emergency if there is fast breathing, chest indrawing, blue lips, inability to feed, lethargy, or noisy breathing.  
The child should be taken immediately to the nearest hospital/clinic for assessment of oxygen level, chest examination, and treatment such as oxygen, nebulized salbutamol if wheezing, antibiotics if pneumonia is suspected, steroids for croup/asthma, or urgent removal of a foreign body if choking is suspected.  
Do not give cough syrups, sedatives, antibiotics, or herbal mixtures without a clinician’s prescription, as they may delay proper treatment or harm the child.  
While going to hospital, keep the child sitting upright, loosen tight clothing, keep the airway clear, and continue breastfeeding/small fluids only if the child can swallow safely.  
Advise the mother to avoid smoke and dust exposure, complete immunizations, ensure good nutrition, and seek care early whenever cough is associated with fever, fast breathing, chest indrawing, poor feeding, or worsening symptoms.

question: Arabinrin ọmọ ogbon odun lo bimọ bi iṣẹju merinlelogbon seyin a sọ pe bi ṣe rọrun nigba ti arabinrin yii bi ọmọ rẹ omo naa n sun ju o nira fun gan lati ke ko si ṣe daada ọmọ naa ko sunkun pupọ lẹsẹkẹsẹ nigbati a bi tan o si dabi ẹni pe o nira fun lati ji Àwọ̀ ara rẹ̀ dá bí ẹni pé ó fẹ́ sán kò gbé apá rẹ̀ àti ẹsẹ̀ rẹ̀ dáadáa bó ṣe yẹ kó gbún lè jẹun torí wípé ó ń sùn jù kò sì lè fa ọmú dáadáa ìyá ọmọ náà ṣe àníyàn wípé àwọn ọmọ òun tó bí tẹ́lẹ̀ kété tí òun bá bí wọn tán, wọ́n máa ń sunkún lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ yìí? reference:

model_answer:
This baby has danger signs of neonatal depression/birth asphyxia and must be managed as an emergency, not just allowed to sleep.  
Immediately dry and keep the baby warm, position the head, clear the airway only if blocked, stimulate gently, check breathing and heart rate, and start bag-mask ventilation if not breathing well or heart rate is below 100/min; add oxygen if available and give chest compressions if heart rate remains below 60/min after effective ventilation.  
Assess Apgar score, temperature, weight/gestational age, oxygen saturation, heart rate, respiratory effort, tone, colour, and check blood glucose urgently; if glucose is low or baby cannot suck, give IV 10% dextrose according to protocol.  
Do not force breastfeeding until stable; give expressed breast milk by cup/tube only when breathing is safe, and consider IV fluids, antibiotics if infection risk, and monitoring for seizures or hypoxic brain injury.  
The baby should be referred/admitted urgently to a newborn unit or hospital with neonatal resuscitation and oxygen support.

model_answer:
Bluish lips/mouth in a newborn with difficulty breathing, especially during breastfeeding, is a danger sign called cyanosis and needs urgent hospital care immediately.  
Possible causes include serious congenital heart disease, newborn pneumonia/sepsis, airway obstruction, aspiration, or problems from birth, and these cannot be safely diagnosed or treated at home.  
Stop feeding when the baby is struggling, keep the baby warm, place the baby on the side or upright, and go to the nearest hospital/emergency unit now for oxygen and assessment.  
The baby should have oxygen saturation checked, blood sugar, infection assessment, chest examination/X-ray if needed, and possibly an echocardiogram to check the heart.  
Do not give herbal medicine or over-the-counter drugs; delay can be fatal in a newborn with cyanosis.

Kí ló fa tí ó fi ń yẹra fún àwọn ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ̀ lójijì?
Ṣé ó lè jẹ́ ìṣòro bí ìbànújẹ́, ìfẹ̀sùn ọkàn, tàbí àníyàn?
Báwo ni a ṣe lè ràn án lọ́wọ́ kí inú rẹ̀ lè dùn sí i?
Àwọn àmì ìkìlọ̀ wo la gbọ́dọ̀ máa ṣọ́ra fún?
Ṣé ó yẹ kí ó rí olùgbani-nímọ̀ràn tàbí amòye ìlera ọpọlọ?
model_answer:
Her sudden withdrawal, loss of interest, low mood, tiredness, and avoiding food/friends may suggest depression, anxiety, stress, trauma, bullying, substance use, or another medical problem, so take it seriously and approach her gently without blaming or forcing her.  
Ask open questions, listen calmly, reassure her she is not alone, encourage regular sleep, meals, light exercise, and gradual contact with trusted family or friends.  
She should see a trained counsellor, clinical psychologist, or mental health professional; if access is limited, start with a trusted doctor at the nearest clinic/hospital who can assess for medical causes and refer appropriately.  
Warning signs needing urgent help include talking about death or suicide, self-harm, giving away belongings, severe hopelessness, refusing to eat/drink, hearing voices, extreme agitation, violence, substance misuse, or suspected abuse.  
If any suicide risk is present, do not leave her alone—remove dangerous objects/medicines and take her immediately to an emergency unit or contact local emergency/mental health services.

These symptoms—excessive thirst, frequent urination especially at night, tiredness and blurred vision—are very suggestive of diabetes mellitus, though urine infection, kidney problems, high calcium, or some medicines can also cause similar symptoms.  
High blood pressure alone usually does not cause this pattern unless it has affected the kidneys or he is taking diuretic “water tablets.”  
He should go to a hospital or clinic promptly for random/fasting blood sugar, HbA1c, urine test for sugar/ketones/infection, kidney function/electrolytes, and blood pressure check.  
Until he is seen, he should avoid sugary drinks, alcohol, sweetened tea, energy drinks, and large portions of refined carbohydrates, but he should continue drinking clean water and eat balanced meals with vegetables, beans, fish/lean protein, and controlled portions of swallow/rice/yam.  
If he has vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, deep fast breathing, fruity breath, severe weakness, or cannot keep fluids down, take him to emergency immediately because very high sugar can be dangerous.

model_answer:
A 7-day-old baby who cannot suck well or gets tired quickly needs urgent assessment today at a hospital or newborn clinic, because poor feeding can be an early sign of infection, low blood sugar, jaundice, breathing problems, tongue-tie, or poor latch.  
If the baby has fever or feels cold, fast/difficult breathing, unusual sleepiness, yellow eyes/skin, vomiting, convulsions, or fewer wet nappies, go to emergency immediately.  
While going, keep the baby warm with skin-to-skin contact and try expressing breast milk to give small amounts with a clean spoon or cup; avoid water, herbs, or other feeds unless advised by a clinician.  
A nurse or doctor should also watch a breastfeed to correct positioning and latch, and check the baby’s mouth, weight, temperature, breathing, and blood sugar.  
This is unlikely to be from “pulling your body” alone; newborn poor feeding should not be managed at home.

model_answer:
Your symptoms after delivery—fever/chills, body weakness, and foul-smelling vaginal bleeding/discharge—strongly suggest puerperal sepsis, an infection of the womb or birth canal, and this is an emergency.  
Simply bathing with clean water usually does not cause this, but putting water, herbs, soap, or fingers inside the vagina, retained placenta/blood clots, tears, or germs during delivery can lead to infection.

Immediate investigations must include a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis, blood cultures, and a malaria rapid test to rule out endemic co-infections. Without delaying for laboratory results, immediately initiate empiric intravenous ceftriaxone or high-dose penicillin, alongside intravenous dexamethasone to reduce severe neurological complications. Provide supportive care with intravenous fluids for hydration and paracetamol to manage the severe headache and any associated fever. Additionally, notify local public health authorities immediately, as meningococcal meningitis is a highly contagious, notifiable disease requiring contact tracing and prophylactic antibiotics for close contacts.

model_answer: The infant's symptoms of fatiguing during feeds, profuse head sweating, and respiratory distress are classic clinical signs of congenital heart disease leading to congestive heart failure. In our community settings where routine neonatal cardiac screening is often unavailable, such presentations require immediate referral for an echocardiogram to identify structural defects like a ventricular septal defect. Initial management should include administering diuretics like furosemide to relieve breathing difficulty and providing high-calorie expressed breast milk via a nasogastric tube to ensure adequate nutrition without physical exertion. Parents must be counseled that prompt medical or surgical intervention is critical to prevent severe failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory infections, and early mortality.

Keep small objects and nuts away from young children to prevent choking, and never leave the child unattended while eating. Seek immediate hospital care whenever a child struggles to breathe, turns bluish, or cannot cry or speak, as these are danger signs requiring emergency treatment.

However, a few months ago, she began to experience severe lower abdominal pain. One day, the pain became so intense that she could hardly stand up properly. **Causes of severe lower abdominal pain in pregnancy:** The combination of sudden severe pain with heavy bleeding most strongly suggests **placental abruption** (premature separation of the placenta), but other causes include ectopic pregnancy (early), miscarriage, preterm labour, uterine rupture, or placenta praevia. Non-obstetric causes like appendicitis, urinary tract infection, or fibroid degeneration can also occur.

**Is all bleeding dangerous?** No—light spotting can be harmless (implantation or after intercourse), but any heavy bleeding, or bleeding with pain, is a **danger sign requiring urgent hospital care**, as it may threaten both mother and baby.

**Warning signs a pregnancy is in trouble:** Severe abdominal pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, passing clots or tissue, fever, reduced or absent fetal movements, severe headache with blurred vision, dizziness or fainting, gush of fluid, and painful contractions before term.

**Medication:** There is **no safe self-medication** to stop pain and bleeding at home—doing so is dangerous and can delay life-saving treatment. Management depends on the cause and requires hospital assessment (ultrasound, blood tests); doctors may give IV fluids, blood transfusion, medications to relax the uterus, or perform emergency delivery/caesarean section as needed—so **immediate hospital care is essential**.

# Newborn with Poor Cry, Stiffness, and Feeding Difficulty

## Likely Causes
This picture suggests **birth asphyxia (hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy)**, which is the most common cause of a depressed newborn who fails to cry and has abnormal tone after delivery. Other important causes to consider are **neonatal sepsis/meningitis, hypoglycaemia, intracranial bleed (birth trauma), congenital abnormalities, or maternal drug effects** (e.g. anaesthesia/sedation given to mother).

## Investigations
Check **blood glucose (glucometer immediately)**, **SpO₂/oxygen saturation**, full blood count, blood culture, serum electrolytes, calcium, and bilirubin. Where available, do a **cranial ultrasound, blood gases, and lumbar puncture** if sepsis or meningitis is suspected.

## Emergency Steps (Resuscitation)
Begin **newborn resuscitation immediately using the HBB approach**: keep the baby **warm (dry, skin-to-skin or warmer)**, **clear the airway (position head, suction mouth then nose)**, and **stimulate** by rubbing the back. If not breathing after stimulation, start **bag-and-mask ventilation with room air/oxygen** within the "Golden Minute," and give **chest compressions** if heart rate stays below 60 despite good ventilation.

## Further Management
Give **oxygen**, correct **hypoglycaemia (IV dextrose)**, start **IV antibiotics** if sepsis is suspected, control seizures with **phenobarbitone** if present, and support feeding via **nasogastric tube or IV fluids** since the baby cannot suck. **Refer urgently to a facility with a newborn special care unit (SCBU/NICU)** for continued monitoring and care.

## Possible Causes
This woman is likely experiencing **secondary postpartum hemorrhage** (bleeding occurring from 24 hours to 6 weeks after delivery). The most common causes are:

3. **Antibiotics** — if infection is present (e.g., ampicillin plus metronidazole).
4. **Ultrasound and possible evacuation (D&C)** — if retained placental tissue is found, it must be removed.
5. **Iron supplements** and good nutrition to help her regain strength after blood loss.

## Advice
Tell the mother that this is a **serious, life-threatening emergency**, and her daughter must not stay at home — she should come to the hospital **now**, not wait. Encourage her to eat iron-rich foods (green vegetables, liver, beans, eggs), rest, and take prescribed medicines. # Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) - Assessment and Management

## Most Likely Cause
This is **primary postpartum hemorrhage**, and the most common cause (about 70% of cases) is **uterine atony** — the uterus failing to contract after delivery. # Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) Management

## What is causing this heavy bleeding?
This is **primary postpartum hemorrhage** (bleeding >500ml within 24 hours of delivery). The most common causes are remembered as the **4 Ts**:
- **Tone** (70%) – uterine atony (uterus failing to contract) is the leading cause
- **Trauma** – tears of the cervix, vagina, or perineum
- **Tissue** – retained placenta or membranes (a second baby is unlikely if not detected on abdominal exam, but retained placenta is common)
- **Thrombin** – clotting disorders

## Immediate steps to take NOW
1. **Call for help** and start resuscitation: two large IV lines, give warmed normal saline/Ringer's lactate rapidly.
2. **Rub up the fundus** (bimanual uterine massage) – if the uterus is soft/boggy, this confirms atony.
3. **Check the placenta is complete** and inspect the birth canal for tears using good light.
4. **Empty the bladder** (catheterize) as a full bladder prevents contraction.
5. **Monitor** pulse, blood pressure, and blood loss continuously.

## Medications (Uterotonics)
- **Oxytocin** 10 IU IM, then infusion 20–40 IU in 1L fluid – first line
- **Misoprostol** 800mcg sublingual/rectal if oxytocin unavailable
- **Ergometrine** 0.5mg IM (AVOID if hypertensive/pre-eclamptic)
- **Tranexamic acid** 1g IV over 10 minutes – give early
- Repair any tears found.

## If bleeding continues
Apply **bimanual uterine compression**, consider **aortic compression** or a **condom uterine balloon tamponade** (locally improvised and effective). Give **antishock garment** if available.

## Referral
**Yes, arrange urgent referral** if bleeding does not stop after these measures, while continuing resuscitation and uterine compression during transport. **Cross-match blood and transfuse** if available before/during transfer. Do NOT delay—start treatment immediately as PPH is a leading cause of maternal death.

# Dog Bite Management - Rabies Risk Assessment

## What Could Happen to the Child
This is a **serious medical emergency** because the dog was unvaccinated and free-roaming, making rabies a real threat. If rabies virus entered the wound, it can travel through the nerves to the brain, causing an infection that is **almost 100% fatal once symptoms appear**. The redness and swelling you observed indicate a **bacterial wound infection** is already developing, which is separate from but can occur alongside rabies risk.

## Immediate Wound Care
Wash the wound **thoroughly with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes** — this is the single most effective step to reduce rabies virus. Apply an antiseptic like povidone-iodine or alcohol afterward. Do **not** suture the wound tightly, as this can trap the virus.

## Vaccines and Medications Needed
1. **Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)** — give the rabies vaccine series (days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28) immediately.
2. **Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG)** — infiltrate around the wound if the child has never been vaccinated before; this is critical for this high-risk bite.
3. **Tetanus vaccine/toxoid** — give if immunization is not up to date, plus tetanus immunoglobulin if needed.
4. **Antibiotics** — start amoxicillin-clavulanate to treat and prevent the bacterial infection causing the redness and swelling.

## Additional Steps
Try to **observe or locate the dog for 10 days** — if it remains alive and healthy, rabies is unlikely, but **do not delay vaccinating the child** while waiting. Monitor the wound daily for spreading infection, pus, or fever, and clean it regularly. There is no reliable blood test to confirm rabies before symptoms, so treatment is based on the exposure risk. **Start the rabies vaccine today without delay** — do not wait for symptoms, as it is too late to treat once they begin.

# Newborn with Cyanosis and Feeding Difficulty

**Why the lips change color:** Bluish discoloration of the lips (cyanosis) means the baby's blood is not carrying enough oxygen. In a newborn who turns blue during feeding, this strongly suggests **congenital heart disease** (a "blue baby" condition like Tetralogy of Fallot or transposition), not liver disease. Liver disease does not cause cyanosis in this way.

**Is difficulty breathing during feeding dangerous?** Yes, this is a serious danger sign. Feeding requires effort, and a baby with heart or lung disease cannot breathe adequately while sucking, so they stop, tire quickly, sweat, and turn blue.

**Other danger signs parents must watch for:** Fast breathing (>60/min), chest indrawing, grunting, nasal flaring, sweating during feeds, poor weight gain, cold clammy skin, lethargy, refusing to feed, fever or low temperature, and worsening blue color of lips, tongue, or nail beds.

**Emergency management:** Give **oxygen** immediately, keep the baby warm, position the airway (knee-to-chest position helps in cyanotic heart disease), stop feeding during episodes, and establish IV access. Urgently refer to a facility with a pediatrician/cardiologist for echocardiography, and prostaglandin (PGE1) may be needed to keep the ductus open in duct-dependent heart lesions—so **do not delay hospital referral**.

# Likely Cause and Clinical Guidance

## Most Probable Diagnosis
The child most likely has **bronchial asthma**, given the persistent cough that worsens at night, wheezing (the "whistling" sound in the chest during breathing), and difficulty breathing. Nighttime worsening is a classic feature of asthma. Other possibilities to consider include **whooping cough (pertussis)**, especially if the cough comes in severe fits, or a **lower respiratory tract infection like bronchiolitis** in younger children.

## Danger Signs to Watch For
Take the child to hospital urgently if you notice: fast or laboured breathing, chest indrawing (skin sucking in below the ribs), bluish lips or tongue, inability to feed or drink, drowsiness or unresponsiveness, high fever, or breathing so difficult the child cannot speak or cry.

## Triggers to Avoid
Avoid smoke (cooking fire, cigarettes, mosquito coils), dust, cold air, strong perfumes, and known allergens like animal dander. Keep the home well ventilated and the child's sleeping area clean and free of dust.

## Action
Please take the child to hospital for proper assessment; the doctor may prescribe an inhaler (like salbutamol) and check whether infection is present, as asthma requires proper treatment and follow-up.

# Managing Pre-eclampsia to Prevent Progression to Eclampsia

This patient shows classic signs of **pre-eclampsia** — high blood pressure, persistent headache, visual disturbances (dishi-dishi), facial and limb swelling, and general weakness in pregnancy — which can progress to eclampsia (seizures) if not properly managed.

## Additional Steps for Management

1. **Test urine for protein (proteinuria)** — this confirms pre-eclampsia and helps assess severity; use dipstick or 24-hour urine collection.
2. **Order blood tests** — full blood count (platelets), liver enzymes (AST/ALT), kidney function (creatinine, urea), and uric acid to check for HELLP syndrome or severe disease.
3. **Give Magnesium Sulphate (MgSO4)** — this is the essential drug to prevent seizures/eclampsia in severe pre-eclampsia; it is life-saving and widely available in Nigerian facilities.
4. **Refer to a hospital with specialist and neonatal care** — severe pre-eclampsia often requires close monitoring and possibly delivering the baby, as **delivery is the definitive cure**.
5. **Monitor the baby** — check fetal wellbeing with fetal heart rate and ultrasound (growth, fluid).

## Prevention (What the Woman Can Do)

- **Attend antenatal care (ANC) early and regularly** so blood pressure is checked at every visit.
- Take **low-dose aspirin** from early pregnancy if she has risk factors (advised by her doctor).
- Ensure adequate **calcium intake**, rest, and reduced stress.
- **Report warning signs immediately** — headache, blurred vision, swelling, or upper abdominal pain.

Early ANC attendance and prompt reporting of symptoms are the most effective ways to prevent progression to eclampsia.

**Nasal congestion in a newborn (likely from normal nasal secretions or mild upper respiratory infection).**

Your baby's difficulty feeding and "snoring/blocked nose" breathing is almost always caused by **nasal congestion**, because newborns are obligate nose-breathers—they must breathe through the nose while sucking, so a blocked nose forces them to stop feeding to breathe through the mouth. Common causes include mild viral cold (mura), thick mucus, dried secretions, dry or dusty air, or lingering amniotic fluid in the airways after birth, which is usually harmless and clears on its own.

**What to do:** Put 1–2 drops of clean saline (salt water: quarter teaspoon salt in a cup of cooled boiled water) in each nostril before feeds, then gently suck out mucus with a bulb syringe; breastfeed frequently in a slightly upright position, and keep the room free of smoke and dust.

# Whooping Cough (Pertussis) - Likely Diagnosis

## Possible Causes
The severe cough with paroxysms that interrupt breathing, followed by difficulty breathing, strongly suggests **whooping cough (pertussis)**, caused by *Bordetella pertussis*. Other considerations include **foreign body aspiration**, **severe bronchiolitis** (RSV), **pneumonia**, or **asthma**. The characteristic pattern of coughing fits ending in a "whoop" or vomiting, often with a color change, points most toward pertussis, especially in an under-immunized child.

## Investigations
- **Nasopharyngeal swab** for PCR or culture of *B. pertussis* (most confirmatory)
- **Full blood count** — lymphocytosis is typical in pertussis
- **Chest X-ray** to exclude pneumonia, foreign body, or "shaggy heart" sign
- **Oxygen saturation (pulse oximetry)** to assess breathing severity

## Treatment
- **Macrolide antibiotics**: azithromycin (10 mg/kg day 1, then 5 mg/kg days 2–5) or erythromycin
- **Supportive care**: oxygen if saturation is low, adequate hydration, and small frequent feeds
- **Hospital admission** if the child is under 6 months, has apnea, cyanosis, or feeding difficulty

## Advice to the Caregiver
Ensure the child completes routine immunizations (DPT/pentavalent vaccine) and vaccinate other household contacts. Keep the child calm, feed small amounts frequently, and seek urgent care immediately if breathing stops, lips turn blue, or the child cannot feed. Household contacts may need preventive antibiotics, and the child should be isolated to prevent spread.

# Assessment of Newborn with Cyanosis and Feeding Difficulty

**What causes the bluish (cyanotic) lips?** The bluish discoloration around the mouth and lips indicates **cyanosis**, meaning the baby's blood is not carrying enough oxygen. In a newborn, this strongly suggests a **congenital heart defect** (cyanotic heart disease such as Transposition of the Great Arteries, Tetralogy of Fallot) or a serious respiratory/airway problem.

**Why does the baby struggle and gasp during feeding?** The worsening cyanosis and respiratory distress specifically during feeding is highly suggestive of **choanal atresia** (blockage of the nasal passages) — newborns are obligate nose breathers, so they turn blue when feeding but improve when crying. It could also reflect a heart defect where feeding increases oxygen demand the heart cannot meet.

**Can medicine be given, or must the baby be examined?** This is a **medical emergency** — you cannot simply give medicine. The baby must be **urgently examined and referred**, checking oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter (pre- and post-ductal), listening for heart murmurs, and attempting to pass a catheter through each nostril to rule out choanal atresia. Refer immediately to a facility with newborn/cardiac care for further investigation (echocardiogram, chest X-ray) and definitive treatment.

# Emergency Assessment: Third-Trimester Bleeding with Severe Abdominal Pain

**1. Possible Cause of Severe Abdominal Pain and Heavy Bleeding:**
The most likely cause is **placental abruption (abruptio placentae)** — premature separation of the placenta, which presents with sudden severe abdominal pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, a tense/rigid uterus, and signs of shock. Placenta previa is another possibility but is usually painless; uterine rupture must also be considered.

**2. Immediate Actions:**
This is an **obstetric emergency**. Secure two large-bore IV lines, give fast IV fluids (normal saline/Ringer's lactate), lay her on her left side, give oxygen, keep her warm, monitor vital signs and fetal heartbeat, and prepare urgently for possible emergency caesarean section. Cross-match blood and mobilize the surgical/obstetric team immediately.

**3. Investigations:**
Check **full blood count, blood group and cross-match, clotting profile (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen), urea/creatinine/electrolytes**, and do an **abdominal ultrasound** to assess placental position, retroplacental clot, and fetal wellbeing.

**4. Appropriate Treatment:**
Resuscitate with IV fluids and **blood transfusion**; the definitive treatment is **urgent delivery**, usually by emergency caesarean section given severe bleeding and fetal distress. Give tetanus prophylaxis if needed, treat coagulopathy, and administer anti-D immunoglobulin if she is Rhesus negative.

**5. Diet and Hygiene:**
After stabilization she should avoid alcohol, tobacco, and raw/unhygienic foods, and eat iron-rich foods (green vegetables, liver, beans) to recover from blood loss. She should maintain clean perineal hygiene, use clean sanitary pads, and attend follow-up antenatal care.

# Postpartum Fever Management

This woman has postpartum fever (38.2°C) with rigors and body pains, presenting hours after delivery. While her malaria RDT is positive, **fever in the immediate postpartum period must never be attributed to malaria alone** — puerperal sepsis is a leading cause of maternal death in our setting and requires urgent exclusion.

**Critical concerns with your current management:** Paracetamol and oral fluids alone are inadequate. You must promptly assess for sepsis by examining the uterus (tenderness, subinvolution), the lochia (offensive smell suggesting endometritis), any perineal/caesarean wounds, and the breasts (mastitis). Check for excessive bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, and respiratory rate to detect early shock, and remember postpartum pre-eclampsia can also cause this presentation.

**Recommended action:** Start effective antimalarial treatment (artemisinin-based combination therapy if she can tolerate orals, or parenteral artesunate if she is unwell or vomiting), but simultaneously begin broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole) if sepsis cannot be excluded. ## Assessment of the Lethargic Newborn

A newborn who is excessively sleepy, has a weak cry, and poor feeding tone since birth shows **danger signs** that require urgent evaluation, even with normal temperature and breathing. The most likely causes include **maternal sedation from labour medications (e.g., pethidine/opioids), neonatal sepsis, hypoglycaemia, birth asphyxia, or metabolic problems** — sepsis and hypoglycaemia must be excluded immediately.

## Immediate Management

Check **blood glucose** urgently; if low, give expressed breast milk or IV/oral dextrose. If maternal opioids were given during labour, consider **naloxone**. Screen for sepsis and start **empirical IV antibiotics (ampicillin plus gentamicin)** if any suspicion, and keep the baby warm. Do not discharge until the baby is alert, feeding well, and stable.

## Home Advice for the Mother

**Give:** exclusive breastfeeding on demand (at least 8–12 times daily), skin-to-skin contact, and warmth. **Do NOT give:** water, glucose water, herbal concoctions ("madara"/traditional remedies), or any food/drink besides breast milk in the first 6 months, as these cause infection and illness. Watch for danger signs (poor feeding, fever, fast breathing, jaundice) and return promptly.

## Maternal Nutrition

The mother should eat a balanced diet rich in protein (beans, fish, eggs, meat), iron-rich foods (green vegetables, liver), whole grains, fruits, and drink plenty of fluids, while continuing **iron/folate supplements** to support recovery and breast milk production.

# Likely Diagnosis: Meningitis (Meningococcal)

This clinical picture strongly suggests **bacterial meningitis**, most likely **meningococcal meningitis**, given the sudden severe headache, neck stiffness (inability to flex or rotate the neck), and the sudden appearance of a skin rash (petechial/purpuric rash), which is characteristic of meningococcal infection (*Neisseria meningitidis*).

## What the Wife Should Do

1. **Seek emergency medical care immediately** — this is a life-threatening condition requiring urgent hospital treatment with intravenous antibiotics (such as ceftriaxone). Do not delay.

2. **Do not attempt home treatment** — this cannot be managed at home; every hour of delay increases the risk of death or permanent disability.

3. **Isolate and protect close contacts** — meningococcal disease is contagious; the wife and family members may need **prophylactic antibiotics** (e.g., ciprofloxacin or rifampicin) as advised by the doctor.

4. **Report immediately** — in Nigeria, meningitis is common during the dry season, especially in the northern "meningitis belt," and outbreaks are notifiable to public health authorities.

The presence of a rash with neck stiffness is a **medical emergency**, and the man needs a lumbar puncture and immediate antibiotics to survive and recover fully.

# Diagnosis: Hyperthyroidism in Pregnancy (Likely Graves' Disease)

The combination of **rapid heartbeat (tachycardia), fatigue, hand tremors, and anterior neck swelling (goiter)** in this pregnant woman strongly suggests **hyperthyroidism**, most commonly caused by **Graves' disease**, which is the leading cause during pregnancy. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring **TSH (low), free T4 and T3 (high)**, and TSH-receptor antibodies; her doctor should arrange these tests urgently.

## Effects on the Baby
Yes, untreated hyperthyroidism can harm the baby, causing **miscarriage, preterm birth, low birth weight (poor growth/IUGR), stillbirth, and fetal or neonatal thyroid problems**. It also endangers the mother through **pre-eclampsia and heart failure (thyroid storm)**, so treatment (usually **Propylthiouracil in the first trimester**) is essential.

## Danger Signs to Watch at Home
Seek care immediately if she develops: **severe palpitations or chest pain, very high fever, confusion, severe vomiting, breathlessness, swelling of the face/legs, severe headache, or reduced fetal movements**.

## Diet Advice
She should **avoid excess iodine (limit iodized salt, seaweed, kelp) and stimulants like caffeine (strong tea, coffee, energy drinks)**, while eating a **balanced, high-calorie diet rich in protein, fruits, vegetables, and calcium** to support her increased metabolism and the baby's growth. Most importantly, she must attend antenatal clinic promptly for proper testing and medication.

# Secondary Postpartum Hemorrhage

**Likely causes:** Bleeding days to weeks after delivery (secondary postpartum hemorrhage) is most commonly caused by **retained placental fragments** or **endometritis (uterine infection)**, and less commonly by subinvolution of the placental site or clotting problems.

**Immediate management:** She should be examined promptly—check vital signs for shock, palpate the uterus (a soft, tender, enlarged uterus suggests infection or retained tissue), and do a speculum exam; an ultrasound helps confirm retained products, and a full blood count checks the degree of anemia. Give **uterotonics such as oxytocin or misoprostol** to contract the uterus, start **broad-spectrum antibiotics** (e.g., ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole) if infection is suspected, and arrange **evacuation of retained products** if present.

**Restoring her strength:** Treat anemia with **iron and folic acid supplements**, encourage a protein- and iron-rich diet, and give a **blood transfusion** if she is severely anemic or unstable.

**Advice:** Reassure and support her to continue breastfeeding, ensure adequate rest, nutrition, and fluids, and counsel her to return immediately if bleeding, fever, foul-smelling discharge, or weakness worsens.

# Neonatal Emergency: Hypothermia and Sepsis

## What is causing this condition?

This 3-day-old newborn presents with a **medical emergency**, most likely **neonatal sepsis**, which is the leading cause of this clinical picture in our setting. The combination of poor feeding (refusing to breastfeed), lethargy, extreme hypothermia (cold to touch), floppiness (hypotonia), and absent reflexes are classic **danger signs** in a sick neonate. Other possible causes include severe hypoglycemia, birth asphyxia complications, or a serious congenital metabolic/cardiac condition, but sepsis must be treated as the priority until proven otherwise.

## Why is the body so cold?

The severe coldness (**hypothermia**) is a very dangerous sign in a septic newborn. Unlike older children who develop fever with infection, sick neonates often lose their ability to regulate temperature and become cold instead of hot. This hypothermia worsens the situation because it causes poor circulation, low blood sugar, and further reduces the baby's strength — creating a deadly cycle.

## Is poor feeding the only cause?

**No** — refusal to feed is a symptom, not the cause. It reflects a systemic illness (most likely infection) affecting the whole body. Poor feeding, hypothermia, lethargy, and hypotonia together indicate a critically ill baby requiring urgent intervention.

## What should be done?

This baby needs **immediate emergency care**:
- Check and correct blood sugar (give expressed breast milk via nasogastric tube or IV dextrose if unable to feed)
- **Rewarm** the baby using skin-to-skin (kangaroo) care and warm coverings
- Start **IV antibiotics** immediately (e.g., ampicillin + gentamicin) after taking cultures if possible
- Admit and monitor closely, provide oxygen and IV fluids as needed
- Feed via NG tube since the baby cannot suck

## Regarding today's vaccination:

**Postpone the vaccination.** Immunizations should **not** be given to an acutely, severely ill newborn. First stabilize and treat the underlying illness; vaccines can be given once the baby has recovered and is well. Prioritizing life-saving treatment now is the correct clinical decision.

## Likely Diagnosis: Bacterial Meningitis (Meningococcal)

The combination of **sudden severe headache, neck stiffness (unable to turn the neck), photophobia (light hurting the eyes), and a non-tender itchy rash all over the body** strongly suggests **meningococcal meningitis**, a contagious infection caused by *Neisseria meningitidis*. This is a medical emergency and is common in Nigeria's "meningitis belt," especially during the dry season; the rash may represent early meningococcal spread (petechial/purpuric), so it is potentially contagious and requires urgent isolation.

## Recommended Investigations

1. **Lumbar puncture (LP)** — the key test; CSF analysis (cell count, Gram stain, glucose, protein, culture) confirms meningitis and identifies the organism.
2. **Blood cultures, full blood count, and blood glucose.**
3. **CSF/blood PCR or latex agglutination** if available to identify the specific bacteria.

## Treatment Before Results

Do **not** wait for results — start empirical treatment immediately. Give **IV Ceftriaxone** (a single dose can also be used in outbreak settings), and manage the headache and fever supportively. Notify public health authorities and give **prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin or rifampicin)** to close household contacts, as this is a notifiable, contagious disease.

# Assessment of Poor Feeding and Respiratory Distress in an Infant

## Likely Cause
This infant's presentation—**poor feeding, tiring quickly during breastfeeding, sweating on the head/face, and rapid labored breathing**—is highly suggestive of **congestive heart failure**, most commonly from a **congenital heart defect** (such as a ventricular septal defect or other structural problem). Feeding is hard work for a baby, and when the heart cannot pump efficiently, the infant fatigues quickly and sweats due to increased sympathetic drive.

## Is the Breathing a Sign of a Problem?
**Yes.** The rapid, labored, "up-and-down" breathing represents **respiratory distress and tachypnea**, which can result from heart failure, pneumonia, or another respiratory infection—all serious conditions requiring urgent evaluation.

## Danger Signs Parents Should Watch For
- Fast, labored breathing or chest indrawing (retractions)
- Blue color of lips, tongue, or fingertips (cyanosis)
- Grunting sounds, fever, or refusal to feed entirely
- Lethargy, poor weight gain, or reduced urine/wet diapers

## Why the Grunting?
Grunting during feeding is a **compensatory effort to keep the airways open** and improve oxygenation, signaling significant respiratory or cardiac strain.

**The mother did the right thing by seeking care—this baby needs urgent examination, oxygen saturation check, chest assessment, and likely referral for an echocardiogram.**

The husband's symptoms—**morning cough, exertional breathlessness (dyspnea on climbing stairs), and rapid fatigue**—suggest a chronic cardiopulmonary condition. ## Assessment

This woman's presentation—profound weakness, fatigue, dimming/blurred vision, and dizziness shortly after a rapid (precipitous) delivery—is highly suggestive of **postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)** causing hypovolemia and anemia. Precipitous labor is a known risk factor for PPH due to uterine atony and genital tract trauma (tears).

## What to Do First

1. **Assess for ongoing bleeding immediately** — check her vaginal bleeding, palpate the uterus (is it firm and contracted or soft/boggy?), and inspect for perineal, vaginal, or cervical tears. Do NOT assume she is stable just because she delivered.

2. **Check vital signs and estimate blood loss** — measure blood pressure, pulse, and respiratory rate. Tachycardia, hypotension, pallor of conjunctiva/palms, and her symptoms point to significant blood loss.

3. **Immediate management of atony/bleeding** — give a **uterotonic** (oxytocin 10 IU IM, or infusion), perform **uterine massage**, ensure the bladder is empty, and repair any tears. Add tranexamic acid if bleeding is active.

## Blood vs. Food

- **Blood transfusion is the priority** if she has clinical signs of significant hemorrhage (low BP, fast pulse, severe pallor, low estimated hemoglobin). Give **IV fluids (normal saline/Ringer's lactate)** immediately while cross-matching for blood.
- **Food alone will not correct acute blood loss** and is not the answer to her current symptoms—do not rely on feeding to treat this.
- Once stabilized, provide **iron and folate supplementation** and nutritious food for recovery.

**Conclusion:** Yes, she likely lost significant blood and may need transfusion—but first find and stop the source of bleeding, resuscitate with fluids, and transfuse based on her clinical condition and hemoglobin.

# Assessment and Management of Heavy Vaginal Bleeding

## Most Likely Cause
Given her last menstrual period was about 6 weeks ago, the heavy bleeding with pain and clots most likely represents a **miscarriage (incomplete or inevitable abortion)** or an **ectopic pregnancy**, which is a life-threatening emergency. Other causes include hormonal imbalances (dysfunctional uterine bleeding), fibroids, or a molar pregnancy.

## Immediate Emergency Measures
1. **Resuscitate the patient**: Insert two large-bore IV lines and give normal saline or Ringer's lactate rapidly to prevent/treat hypovolemic shock.
2. **Monitor vital signs**: Check blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, and pallor; watch for signs of shock.
3. **Cross-match blood** and transfuse if she is severely anaemic or in shock.
4. Keep her warm, elevate her legs, and give oxygen if needed.

## Medications to Stop the Bleeding
- **Oxytocin** or **misoprostol (400–600 mcg)** to contract the uterus and reduce bleeding if pregnancy-related.
- **Tranexamic acid (1 g IV)** to help reduce heavy bleeding.
- If products of conception are retained, perform **manual vacuum aspiration (MVA)** or evacuation of the uterus.

## Essential Investigations
- **Urine pregnancy test (hCG)** — the single most important first test to confirm pregnancy.
- **Full blood count** to assess degree of anaemia.
- **Pelvic ultrasound** to identify intrauterine pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, retained products, or fibroids.
- **Blood grouping, Rhesus typing, and clotting profile.**

If ectopic pregnancy is confirmed, **urgent surgical intervention (laparotomy)** is required to save her life.

# Placental Abruption (Abruptio Placentae) in a 33-Year-Old at 7 Months Pregnant

**1. Cause of the severe pain and heavy bleeding:**
The most likely cause is **placental abruption** — where the placenta separates from the uterus wall before delivery, causing severe constant abdominal pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, a tense/rigid uterus, and shock. Other possibilities include **placenta praevia** (usually painless bleeding) or **uterine rupture**, but the severe pain plus bleeding points strongly to abruption.

**2. What to do immediately:**
This is an **obstetric emergency** — resuscitate at once: put in two large IV lines, give normal saline/Ringer's lactate to fight shock, give oxygen, catheterize to monitor urine, keep her warm, and urgently prepare for possible caesarean section while notifying the obstetric team and blood bank.

**3. Investigations/tests:**
Check **full blood count, blood group and cross-match blood**, **clotting profile (PT, PTT, fibrinogen)** to detect DIC, urea/electrolytes, and do an **urgent ultrasound scan** to confirm the placenta position and check the baby's heartbeat, plus continuous fetal monitoring.

**4. Treatment:**
Give **IV fluids and blood transfusion** to correct blood loss, then **deliver the baby urgently — usually by emergency caesarean section** if bleeding is heavy or the baby is in distress; give steroids for lung maturity if time allows, treat any clotting problem, and watch closely for postpartum haemorrhage after delivery.

**5. Food to avoid and hygiene advice:**
After stabilization, she should eat **iron-rich foods** (green vegetables, liver, beans, eggs) to rebuild her blood, avoid alcohol and smoking, and reduce very salty food if she has high blood pressure; for hygiene she should keep the private area clean, change pads frequently, wash hands before and after, and wipe from front to back to prevent infection.

# Understanding Breast Lumps in Women

A firm lump in the breast can be caused by several conditions, and most of them are **not cancer**. In younger women, the most common cause is a **fibroadenoma**, which is a smooth, firm, painless lump that moves easily under the fingers and is completely harmless. Other common causes include **breast cysts** (fluid-filled sacs), **fibrocystic changes** (lumpy breasts that may swell and become tender before menstruation), and sometimes **infections or abscesses**, especially in breastfeeding women.

**No — not every firm lump means cancer.** In fact, the majority of breast lumps are benign (harmless), but every lump should still be checked by a doctor to be sure, because you cannot tell just by feeling it.

## Warning signs women should watch for and report to a doctor:
- A hard, fixed lump that does not move
- A lump that keeps growing
- Changes in the skin of the breast (dimpling, thickening, or "orange-peel" appearance)
- Nipple that pulls inward or bleeds/discharges (especially blood-stained)
- Swelling or lumps under the armpit
- Persistent breast pain or skin ulcers

**Likely Causes of Your Symptoms:**

- Heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in under one hour) or passing large clots/tissue

# Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) - Assessment and Management

**Most likely cause:** This is primary postpartum hemorrhage, and the most common cause (about 70% of cases) is **uterine atony** — failure of the uterus to contract and clamp down after delivery. Other possibilities to consider using the "4 T's" are retained placental fragments or retained second twin (Tissue), genital tract lacerations/cervical or vaginal tears (Trauma), and clotting disorders (Thrombin).

**Immediate assessment:** Feel the abdomen — if the uterus is soft/boggy, this confirms atony. Check whether the placenta was delivered complete, examine for tears, and rule out a retained twin. Call for help, start two large-bore IV lines, give IV fluids (normal saline/Ringer's lactate), and cross-match blood for transfusion.

**To stop the bleeding:**
- **Uterine massage** and empty the bladder (catheterize).
- **Oxytocin** 10 IU IM or 20–40 IU in IV fluids is first-line.
- **Misoprostol** 800 mcg sublingual/rectal if oxytocin is inadequate.
- **Ergometrine** 0.5 mg IM (avoid if hypertensive) and/or **Tranexamic acid** 1 g IV.
- If bleeding continues, perform **bimanual uterine compression** and consider intrauterine balloon tamponade or non-pneumatic anti-shock garment.

**Referral:** Yes — after starting resuscitation and uterotonics, refer urgently to a higher facility if bleeding persists, since she may need manual removal of placenta, surgical repair, or examination under anesthesia. Do not delay referral, but continue treatment and monitor vital signs during transport.

# Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH)

**Likely cause:** This is secondary postpartum hemorrhage, occurring days after delivery. The most common causes are retained products of conception (placental fragments or membranes left in the uterus), endometritis (infection of the womb lining), or subinvolution of the placental site (the uterus failing to contract and heal properly). Given the heavy bleeding and profound weakness, she may also be significantly anemic and at risk of hemorrhagic shock.

**Treatment:**
- **Resuscitate first:** Secure IV access, give IV fluids (normal saline/Ringer's lactate), and check vital signs. Assess for shock.
- **Uterotonics:** Give oxytocin or misoprostol to help the uterus contract and reduce bleeding.
- **Antibiotics:** If infection (endometritis) is suspected—fever, foul-smelling lochia, uterine tenderness—start broad-spectrum antibiotics.
- **Evacuate retained products:** If ultrasound or examination confirms retained tissue, perform manual removal or uterine evacuation (D&C).
- **Correct anemia:** Check hemoglobin; arrange blood transfusion if severely anemic, and give iron supplements.

- Check **urine for protein** (proteinuria confirms pre-eclampsia), plus blood tests (full blood count, liver function, kidney function/creatinine, and platelets to rule out HELLP syndrome).

# Understanding a Breast Lump

**What can cause a hard lump in a woman's breast?**

Not all breast lumps mean cancer—in fact, most breast lumps are benign (non-cancerous), especially in younger women. Common causes include fibroadenomas (smooth, firm, movable lumps common in young women), fibrocystic changes (lumpy, sometimes tender areas that change with the menstrual cycle), simple cysts (fluid-filled sacs), or infections/abscesses. However, some lumps can be breast cancer, which is why every persistent lump should be evaluated by a doctor.

**Warning signs to watch for:**

She should be concerned and seek prompt medical attention if the lump is hard, irregular, fixed (not moving), and painless. Other danger signs include: changes in breast size or shape, dimpling or puckering of the skin (like an orange peel), nipple retraction (pulling inward), blood or unusual discharge from the nipple, skin redness or scaling, and swelling under the arm or around the collarbone.

**My advice:** She did the right thing by deciding to see a doctor. She needs a proper examination and possibly an ultrasound, mammogram, or biopsy to determine the exact cause—early detection greatly improves outcomes if it is cancer, and provides reassurance if it is benign.

**Investigations:** Perform a nasopharyngeal swab for *Bordetella pertussis* (culture/PCR), full blood count (lymphocytosis supports pertussis), chest X-ray, and pulse oximetry to assess oxygenation.

**Treatment:** Give a macrolide antibiotic such as **azithromycin** (or erythromycin), provide oxygen if saturation is low, ensure adequate hydration and nutrition, and admit young or severely affected infants for close monitoring.

Based on your description, your husband's symptoms—difficulty breathing, wheezing (whistling sound), and frequent sneezing triggered by dust, smoke, and frying fumes—strongly suggest **allergic asthma** or an allergic respiratory condition.

**Tests that can be done:**
- **Spirometry (lung function test)** to confirm asthma and assess how well his lungs are working.

- **Chest X-ray** to rule out other lung conditions.

**Treatment:** He should see a doctor, but common medications include a **reliever inhaler (salbutamol/Ventolin)** for immediate breathlessness, and a **preventer inhaler (inhaled corticosteroid like beclomethasone)** used daily to control inflammation.

# Diagnosis and Home Care for Nighttime Cough with Breathing Difficulty in an 8-Month-Old

**Most likely cause:** This 8-month-old's symptoms—nighttime cough worsening at night, rapid and labored breathing, and poor feeding—strongly suggest **bronchiolitis**, commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), or possibly early pneumonia. Bronchiolitis typically affects infants under one year and worsens at night due to airway inflammation and mucus accumulation.

**Warning signs requiring urgent care:** The fast breathing, chest struggling (indrawing), and refusal to breastfeed are **danger signs**. Poor feeding indicates the child may be tiring or becoming dehydrated, so the mother was right to seek medical attention promptly.

**Home care measures the mother can take:**
1. Continue frequent breastfeeding in small amounts to maintain hydration.
2. Keep the baby's nose clear using saline drops and gentle suction to ease breathing and feeding.
3. Elevate the head slightly during sleep and keep the room free of smoke and dust.
4. Monitor breathing rate and watch for worsening signs (chest indrawing, bluish lips, or persistent refusal to feed)—these require immediate return to hospital.

**Important:** Avoid over-the-counter cough medicines in infants, as they are unsafe and ineffective at this age. If breathing difficulty worsens, professional evaluation with possible oxygen support is essential.

# Cyanosis in a Newborn During Feeding

**Cause of blue lips (cyanosis):** The bluish discoloration of the lips indicates low oxygen in the blood, and when this occurs specifically during feeding it strongly suggests a congenital heart defect (such as Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, or other cyanotic heart disease) or a respiratory problem. Yes, both heart disease and lung disease can cause the baby to struggle to breathe—feeding increases the baby's oxygen demand and effort, so an underlying cardiac or pulmonary defect will worsen the cyanosis during breastfeeding.

**Other danger signs parents should watch for:** Fast or difficult breathing, chest indrawing (recession), grunting, poor feeding or refusal to feed, lethargy, fever or low body temperature, persistent vomiting, convulsions, yellow skin/eyes (jaundice), and sweating or tiring during feeds.

**Immediate treatment:** Take the baby to hospital urgently, give oxygen, keep the baby warm and calm, and position appropriately; the doctors will do a full examination, pulse oximetry, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram to confirm the diagnosis and provide specific treatment (which may include medications like prostaglandins for certain heart defects or referral for surgical correction).

**This clinical picture strongly suggests preterm labour rather than miscarriage.**

At 6 months (approximately 26 weeks), a viable pregnancy is beyond the miscarriage threshold, so we call this preterm labour, not abortion. The signs pointing to labour include: persistent, regular strong lower abdominal and back pain (contractions), rupture of membranes (watery fluid), and a "show" (blood-stained mucus discharge). In a primigravida (first pregnancy), these findings—regular painful contractions with ruptured membranes and cervical show—are classic for established preterm labour. # Likely Diagnosis: Congenital Heart Disease (Heart Failure in an Infant)

This clinical picture—poor feeding, fatigue and stopping after only a few sucks, sweating on the head and face during feeding, and rapid labored breathing—strongly suggests **congestive heart failure**, most commonly caused by a **congenital heart defect** (such as a ventricular septal defect or other structural abnormality) in an infant.

**Why the poor feeding and sweating occur:** Feeding is hard physical work for a baby, and a failing heart cannot meet this increased demand, so the infant tires quickly and stops. The sweating (especially on the head/face) reflects excess sympathetic nervous system activity as the body struggles to compensate for the poor cardiac output.

**Danger signs to watch for immediately:** Fast breathing (over 60 breaths/minute), grunting, chest indrawing, bluish lips or tongue (cyanosis), poor weight gain, lethargy, cold/clammy skin, and difficulty completing feeds.
